title: Female Garment Workers Gain Economic Agency
reason: The core phenomenon is real and well documented: Bangladesh's export garment industry became overwhelmingly female-staffed and is one of the most cited case studies in development economics for export-led female empowerment (delayed marriage/childbirth, schooling gains, household bargaining power — see Kabeer & Mahmud 2004; Heath & Mobarak 2015, J. Dev. Econ.). However, the headline magnitude in the event ('approximately two million women employed... by the mid-1990s') is materially overstated. Primary BGMEA data reproduced in Kabeer & Mahmud's peer-reviewed chapter show female RMG employment of only ~1.08 million in 1994-95, ~1.17 million in 1995-96, and ~1.26 million in 1996-97 (total sector employment 1.2-1.4 million, ~90% female) — roughly 40-45% below the claimed 'two million.' Female employment did not approach ~2 million until roughly a decade later (total sector employment was still only ~1.8 million as late as 2000-01). So the qualitative story (country, year window, and the empowerment narrative) holds, but the quantitative headline is off by a wide margin — a wrong-magnitude PARTIAL rather than TRUE. The comparative claim ('highest share of female industrial employment in South Asia') is plausible given the ~85-90% female share but was not independently corroborated with a South-Asia-wide comparison.
